A.title: Brazil Court Ends CDA Gaming's Betting Reprieve
A.excerpt: A regional court president has suspended CDA Gaming's injunction, signalling that court-by-court exceptions to Brazil's betting ban won't hold.
body: On 6 November 2026 Brazil's Attorney General's Office (AGU) announced that the president of the Federal Regional Court of the 3rd Region had suspended the court-granted authorisation that allowed CDA Gaming, operator of the Casa de Apostas, Bet Sul and Jogo Online brands, to keep offering online fixed-odds betting. The decision ended a short-lived reprieve from the nationwide prohibition that took effect on 5 November, and it is the clearest signal yet that judicial carve-outs from Provisional Measure 1.394 will be contested aggressively by the federal government and, so far, reversed on appeal.

The background matters to anyone advising operators in the market. Provisional Measure 1.394, published on 25 September 2026, bans fixed-odds lottery betting nationwide, including offers made from abroad to persons in Brazil. As reported, sites were required to go offline ten days after publication, existing authorisations lapse thirty days after publication without refund or compensation, and payment institutions are restricted from processing betting transactions. CDA Gaming held an authorisation dated 7 February 2025, published on 11 February 2025 and running to 31 December 2029, so its position was that a validly issued multi-year authorisation could not be extinguished by executive instrument without compensation.

A federal appellate judge, Adriana Pileggi, accepted enough of that argument to grant CDA interim relief. The AGU appealed, and the court president, Johonsom Di Salvo, granted the appeal. His reasoning, as reported, rests on the public interest rather than the merits of the licence dispute: keeping an individual exception in place posed a serious risk to public order, legal certainty and the effectiveness of national betting regulation, and the measure's rules should apply uniformly to all operators. He characterised isolated court exceptions as a source of regulatory instability incompatible with managing a nationwide public policy.

This is a suspension of the interim relief, not a final judgment. The suspension lasts until final judgment in the original case or a later decision by the court presidency, so CDA retains its underlying claim. The practical effect, however, is that the operator is out of the market while the merits are litigated, which is typically years. The order also extends to CDA the logic of the 10 October 2026 decision that barred Stake Brasil from operating after a São Paulo federal court had allowed it to continue provisionally until 25 October. Two operators with different fact patterns have now lost the same procedural contest at the same level.

For counsel, the lesson is about the vehicle used to seek protection. Presidential suspension of injunctions is a well-established mechanism in Brazilian procedure for protecting the public order, public health, public security and public economy, and it is deployed precisely where a lower-court decision has system-wide effects. An injunction that benefits one licensee in a market-wide prohibition is an unusually easy target for that tool. Operators weighing similar applications should assume the AGU will invoke it, and should prepare evidence on the specific, non-systemic character of their position rather than relying on the strength of their licence alone.

The wider constitutional picture remains unsettled. The Supreme Federal Court is separately examining the new rules in three direct constitutional challenges, and a ruling there could reshape the entire landscape regardless of what happens in individual injunction fights. Until then, the economic arguments that operators and trade associations have raised, including the treatment of lawfully licensed businesses that paid substantial fees and committed to compliance programmes, will be tested in the form of compensation claims and constitutional challenges rather than operating relief. Those with licence-fee and grant-payment exposure should be documenting their losses now.

Practical steps follow. Licensed operators should confirm that geoblocking, payment-channel shutdown and customer-communication protocols meet the measure's deadlines, because continued offers after the cut-off will be treated as illegal betting, with the associated domain blocking and payment-freeze consequences seen elsewhere in Brazil's enforcement toolkit. Suppliers, affiliates and payment providers need to review contract termination, refund and indemnity clauses. Brazilian gambling specialists such as Pinheiro Neto Advogados and Mattos Filho are tracking the Supreme Federal Court challenges and the compensation question, and operators with Brazilian exposure should take local advice before relying on any interim court order.

GamblingLawyers.com will continue to follow the CDA, Stake and constitutional-review proceedings. The assessment in this article is based on public reporting of the AGU announcement and is not legal advice; operators should verify the current status of any order with Brazilian counsel before acting.

A.title: CFTC Tells Exchanges: Drop State Geofencing in 30 Days
A.excerpt: New CFTC guidance says exchanges generally cannot exclude eligible traders by state, deepening the clash with US gaming regulators.
body: On 5 November 2026 the Commodity Futures Trading Commission issued interpretive guidance on impartial access to designated contract markets (DCMs). The core message is that DCMs generally may not restrict eligible US participants on the basis of where they live or are located. Exchanges have thirty days, so until roughly early December, either to remove geographic restrictions that conflict with the impartial-access requirements or to explain why compliance is not feasible. For a sector in which state-by-state exclusion has become the main compromise between federally regulated event contracts and state gambling law, the guidance lands squarely on a pressure point.

The legal footing is the Commodity Exchange Act's requirement for competitive, open and efficient markets and Commission Regulation 38.151, which requires access criteria to be impartial, transparent and nondiscriminatory. The CFTC's stated rationale is market-structure based: excluding whole states fragments liquidity, impairs risk management and reduces price discovery, which it says matters particularly for event contracts tied to elections, sports or other geographically concentrated outcomes. The guidance also indicates that exchanges must ensure the intermediaries that route customers to their markets comply with the same principles.

The timing is not accidental. On 25 September 2026 the Sixth Circuit found that Kalshi had not shown its sports event contracts meet the statutory definition of a swap, held that federal law did not preempt Ohio and Tennessee gambling laws, and read impartial access as referring to the markets an exchange offers rather than every contract in every state. The Ninth Circuit has likewise rejected the argument that Nevada's geographic restrictions and federal impartial-access rules necessarily conflict, calling it a false all-or-nothing proposition. The new guidance reads as the CFTC pressing its own interpretation against that appellate reasoning, though guidance does not by itself overturn any court ruling.

The guidance is careful on that point. It does not direct exchanges to disregard contrary court orders, and a DCM that cannot remove restrictions may explain why, with the Commission saying it will weigh the facts and circumstances. That leaves a practical dilemma for operators that are subject to state-court injunctions or cease-and-desist orders while also being told by their federal regulator to open access. The most plausible outcome is a patchwork of explanations filed with the CFTC rather than wholesale removal of geofences, at least while certiorari petitions and state enforcement actions remain pending. Kalshi's response to a New Jersey petition is reportedly due on 7 December.

State regulators and tribal gaming interests will read the guidance as a further assertion of federal primacy over products they regard as sports wagering. A bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general had already urged the Supreme Court to review the dispute in October, and the guidance gives them an additional hook: it concedes, implicitly, that state-level restrictions are what exchanges are currently applying. Expect it to feature in briefs and in legislative testimony, and expect state commissions to consider whether broker, wallet and affiliate relationships that route residents to event-contract markets are within their licensing and advertising jurisdiction.

For compliance teams the analysis divides by role. Exchanges and clearing participants need a documented rationale for each geographic restriction that remains, mapped to the specific order, statute or enforcement risk that requires it. Intermediaries, including brokerages, crypto wallets and sportsbook-affiliated front ends, should assume they fall within the guidance's reach and review whether their own state exclusions are mirrored contractually from the exchange or imposed unilaterally. Licensed sportsbooks that also offer or promote event contracts face a separate exposure: if an exchange opens a state, their gaming licences in that state may be put at risk by association.

Firms such as Ifrah Law, ZwillGen and Holland & Knight advise on the intersection of federal derivatives law and state gambling regimes, and operators should obtain advice specific to their licensing footprint. In the meantime the thirty-day window is the operative date. Anyone contemplating a response to the CFTC, an adjustment to geofencing, or a communication to state regulators should do so with the court-order position in each affected state mapped out first. This article summarises public reporting and is not legal advice.

A.title: VG Halle Pauses GGL Ban Over Deposit-Limit Practice
A.excerpt: An interim ruling finds the GGL's tolerance of SCHUFA checks may undercut Germany's licensing rules under EU law, with a CJEU referral expected.
body: In a decision of 6 August 2026 in case 7 B 491/25, reported by Beck-aktuell on 18 August, the Verwaltungsgericht Halle ordered suspensive effect for a lawsuit brought by a provider of virtual slot-machine games against a prohibition order issued by the Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder (GGL). The court found in summary proceedings that the licensing requirement for brokering virtual slot games likely conflicts with the freedom to provide services under Article 56 TFEU, so the prohibition order probably cannot stand at this stage. It is an interim ruling, not a final decision on the merits, but its reasoning is a roadmap for operators contesting enforcement.

The provider has challenged the order since 2022, and the court had rejected an earlier interim application in 2023. What changed is the court's view of the GGL's enforcement practice. Where it previously saw an enforcement gap, it now sees systematic tolerance flowing from the authority's established administrative practice. That distinction is significant in EU law because the Court of Justice's case law requires the coherence of a gambling restriction to be assessed against how it is actually applied, not only against the wording of the statute.

The focus is the monthly deposit limit. Players may deposit up to EUR 1,000 per month across providers, and a higher limit requires verifiable proof of economic capacity. The GGL's own guidelines call for tax assessments, income proofs or bank statements. In practice, the court found, the authority accepts a SCHUFA-G report, which measures default risk and says little about a player's capacity to bear gambling losses. The court noted that courts, expert bodies and state governments have found the approach unsuitable as a measure of financial capacity.

The court added a second point: that accepting a good credit score in place of proof of means, together with permitting maximum stakes of up to EUR 5 per game, makes it easier for players to lose large sums quickly. In its view that conflicts with the State Treaty's own objectives, particularly player protection. A regulator that systematically weakens the protective measures on which a licensing monopoly depends cannot, at least while it does so, rely on the licensing requirement to justify restricting cross-border services. The court expects in the main proceedings to refer questions to the Court of Justice of the European Union, which is why it granted suspensive effect.

Several caveats apply. The decision is a single first-instance administrative court acting in summary proceedings, and other German courts have repeatedly upheld the GGL's powers and the licensing regime's compatibility with EU law. The ruling is also fact-specific to a prohibition order against a virtual-slot broker, not a general finding that unlicensed offers are lawful. The GGL may appeal, may adjust its practice on income verification, or may argue that the tolerance identified is a transitional matter. Operators should not infer that licensing requirements have been disapplied in Germany.

Even so, the ruling matters for strategy. Any operator or affiliate facing GGL prohibition, payment-blocking or administrative-fine proceedings has a new line of argument that attacks coherence through enforcement practice, supported by evidence of how limits are verified in practice. Licensed operators have the converse interest: if the SCHUFA-based approach is found to be inadequate, they may be required to adopt stricter verification at short notice, with the commercial effect on higher-limit players that would follow. Compliance teams should map the evidence they currently collect for limit increases against the standard in the GGL's guidelines.

A potential CJEU reference would add a European dimension to a long-running national debate, arriving as the State Treaty comes up for review. Specialist counsel including Hambach & Hambach, Redeker Sellner Dahs and CMS Germany have extensive experience in the German regime, and any operator relying on this reasoning should take advice on the procedural posture of its own case. GamblingLawyers.com will monitor appeals and any reference. This article is general commentary and not legal advice.

A.title: Austria's Open Licences: What Legacy Operators Must Meet
A.excerpt: Austria's draft opens online gambling to unlimited licences, but legacy grey-market operators face tax, judgment and cooling-off hurdles.
body: Austria's Ministry of Finance submitted its draft gambling reform to the European Commission on 4 August 2026, starting a mandatory three-month standstill period that runs to roughly early November. With that window now closing, attention turns to the detail of what operators would have to meet to hold an Austrian online licence. According to published law-firm analysis of the consultation draft, the proposal would replace the single-operator online monopoly with an unlimited number of licences, but the conditions are demanding and are drafted with a particular eye to operators that have served Austrian players without a licence.

On structure, initial licences would run for up to five years, with renewals of up to ten years. Licence holders would need to be a stock corporation or limited liability company with a supervisory board, have their seat in Austria or another EU or EEA state, and hold at least EUR 10 million in paid-up share capital. The initial licence fee is reported at EUR 300,000, and applicants must demonstrate regulatory reliability and integrity. The capital requirement is high by European standards and will favour well-capitalised groups over smaller B2C brands.

The legacy-operator provisions are the most distinctive. Applicants that previously offered online gambling in Austria without a licence would have to pay all due and not time-barred Austrian gambling tax, satisfy all final Austrian court judgments obtained by players, and show that final Austrian civil judgments are enforceable in the operator's home jurisdiction. The last requirement goes beyond payment history: it asks for a jurisdictional condition that some offshore licensing regimes may not satisfy. Years of player-restitution litigation in Austria make this an operational and balance-sheet question, not a formality.

A cooling-off mechanism, modelled on the Dutch market-opening approach, reinforces the point. Operators that cease unlicensed activity by 1 January 2027 would face an 18-month exclusion from licensing, while those still active after 31 December 2029 would face 24 months. The design pushes operators out of the grey market before licensing begins, but it also raises a strategic question: whether to exit early and accept a defined wait, or remain and risk a longer exclusion and enforcement exposure. The analysis differs depending on the operator's existing Austrian revenue, outstanding claims and EU licence portfolio.

Player-protection rules are equally prescriptive. Reported deposit caps are EUR 250 per week for players under 26 and EUR 1,680 per month for players aged 26 and over, with a risk-based approach for older age bands and higher limits possible where there is no sign of harm and additional safeguards are in place. Mandatory behavioural monitoring, a central cross-operator exclusion register and operator-wide supervision systems are also proposed. Operators accustomed to the EUR 1,000-type ceilings of other regimes will need to model the revenue effect of such limits before committing to the application fee and capital.

Enforcement is backed by website blocking, payment blocking for transactions linked to illegal operators, public blacklists of unlicensed operators and expanded investigative powers. Payment-service providers, app stores and affiliates should therefore treat the draft as a prelude to a more active enforcement environment, even before licensing starts. Because the draft remains subject to change and must still pass through parliament, the final conditions could differ, and a Commission or member-state comment during the standstill period could trigger amendments.

Our assessment is that the package is designed to deliver tax and player-claim recovery as much as market liberalisation. Prospective applicants should audit their Austrian history now: revenue and tax exposure for prior years, the status of judgments and pending claims, and the enforceability analysis for their home jurisdiction. Corporate-structure work, including the supervisory-board requirement and capital planning, takes time. Austria-focused advisers, including the Austrian practices of CMS, Bird & Bird and Taylor Wessing, can assist, and operators should wait for the final text before filing. This article is commentary on public reporting, not legal advice.

A.title: Gibraltar's Prediction Market Authorisation Regime
A.excerpt: Gibraltar's LN.2026/176 creates a dedicated authorisation for prediction markets, with substance, contract-approval and stablecoin provisions.
body: Gibraltar has created a bespoke regulatory category for prediction markets. The Prediction Market Regulations 2026 (LN.2026/176) came into force on 13 July 2026, made by the minister responsible for gambling under sections 34 and 159 of the Gambling Act 2025. The regulations define prediction market activity as a separate category that is not classed as betting, gaming or a lottery merely because of its characteristics, and they require a prediction market authorisation distinct from a standard gambling licence under Part 4 of the Act. For operators looking for a jurisdiction that positions event contracts outside the traditional gambling box, this is a notable development.

The scope of the exemption and the interaction with existing licensing are carefully drawn. Authorised operators on the official register are exempt from the general prohibition on unlicensed gambling-related activity in section 26 of the Act. Existing gambling licensees must apply separately for prediction market authorisation, while purely prediction-market businesses can apply without holding a general gambling licence. That gives a pathway for fintech and exchange-style entrants that have no wish to build a betting-operator profile.

Schedule 2 sets the core authorisation requirements. Applicants and their controllers must be fit and proper, the business must have a substantive presence in Gibraltar including mind and management expectations, and it must have adequate financial and non-financial resources. The substance requirement echoes the approach in the Gambling Act 2025 more generally and will matter for operators that expected to run a lean local presence. Boards, decision-making and risk functions will need genuine local anchoring, and the regulator will look for evidence rather than assertions.

The product and conduct rules read more like market-infrastructure regulation than a betting code. Only contracts approved by the Authority, or certified under approved arrangements, may be listed. Operators must maintain robust contract rules and reliable, transparent, manipulation-resistant settlement sources, together with market-integrity controls against insider dealing and manipulation, conflict-of-interest management and safeguarding of client money. Compliance with anti-money laundering and sanctions legislation is required. Digital asset payments, including stablecoins, are expressly permitted for funding accounts and settling contracts, which will appeal to crypto-native platforms.

Supervision is split between the Licensing Authority, which grants authorisations, and the Gibraltar Gambling Commissioner, who supervises authorised operators using modified versions of the Act's information-gathering, investigatory and sanctioning powers. Appeals of decisions of the Authority or Commissioner lie to the Supreme Court of Gibraltar within 28 days of service, although certain decisions, including an initial refusal of authorisation, are excluded. The limited appeal right on refusals makes the quality of the first application unusually important.

The commercial context is the global scramble over how prediction markets are classified. US federal and state authorities are in litigation over whether sports event contracts are swaps or gambling, several European regulators have blocked or investigated platforms, and others have no framework at all. A regime that creates certainty on classification, conduct and settlement, backed by an EU-adjacent common-law court system, could attract operators seeking a regulated base outside the US. It will not, however, resolve the question of whether contracts may be offered into other jurisdictions, where local gambling law may still apply to the activity regardless of where the operator is authorised.

That distinction should be at the centre of any market-entry plan. A Gibraltar authorisation addresses Gibraltar law; it does not by itself authorise offers to customers in the United Kingdom, the EU or the United States, and cross-border exposure should be assessed market by market. Gibraltar practitioners, including Isolas and Hassans, advise on the new regime, and applicants should expect a substantive dialogue with the regulator on contract design and settlement sources. This article summarises public commentary on the regulations and is not legal advice.
